Images:

    The text in the image is a response from "Djehuty" to a post, explaining the thought process behind a video featuring a gag with a brown body paint. The text is transcribed as follows:
    
    "Hello there, let me try to clear this up. First up, I think it's perfectly fine that this topic was brought up. Everyone on the WahlBanana team thought seriously about this portrayal before we went ahead with it.
    
    As someone from an international school I've made friends with people of all races and I am also well aware of the racism that some of them face. That's why during our video production we made it a point to make sure the gag didn't offend people.
    
    One of the reasons we decided to go with the brown body paint was that the gag was a visual gag. We didn't want to have any spoken lines during the gag and so we needed to portray the joke visually.
    
    We've portrayed Indian characters in our skits before using just accents and mannerisms but in this case it wasn't possible. We didn't find it wrong to show that Indians and Chinese have different skin colors, it's merely something visual that helps represent the character.
    
    In the end I think racism really all boils down to the meanings behind the words and actions. All of us have heard one or two racist jokes and very likely even enjoyed them. Why? Because we know there is no malicious intent behind them and they are meant in good fun. We also know the people making those jokes don't actually believe them to be true.
    
    Ultimately, when we decided to run this gag, we came to the conclusion that our audience would be mature enough to understand that the intentions behind it was purely for entertainment. I don't think we portrayed Indian foreign workers in a negative light in the video.
    
    On the other hand I understand that some people may be offended. To those people, I sincerely apologize. I have friends from all over the globe and I respect all of them equally no matter what race they are. I would hate to condone any racism.
    
    Like - Reply - 6y"
    
    There are 10 likes on the comment.

title: Singapore’s Brownface Loop: Receipts vs ‘Imported’
summary:
The most brutal throughline is Sharan Kaur’s: Singapore keeps pretending racism complaints are “new” and “Western”… while the archives show people have been calling this out *here* for over a century. Her killer dunk is the 1980s clip: a Black US embassy info officer, Beverly Hendrix, says Darkie toothpaste is discriminatory, a Chinese man “disagrees,” and Sharan’s basically like—cool, we’ve been stuck in this exact 40-year argument on repeat.

This strand kicks off when @visakanv drops a “History of Singaporean Chinese people in Brownface” thread (UOB’s 2012 Bollywood party pics, Wahbanana’s 2013 skit, Desmond Tan’s 2015 IG, Singapore Sports Institute’s Deepavali party, then the 2019 N-Epay ad). The outrage peaks when police reports get filed against YouTuber Preetipls and Subhas Nair *for reacting* to brownface—Visa’s punchline is the state’s logic: “The police will not tolerate any offensive content that causes ill will between races,” said while punishing the people pointing out the offense. Meanwhile, establishment-ish voices do the classic minimisation: Indranee Rajah writes that the Black and White Minstrel Show used to be “quite acceptable,” and Margaret Chan literally argues “brownface is not Singaporean” and the “cosmopolitan” imported the concept. Sharan responds by unloading historical artillery: 1900 Straits Times describing a Chinese man “successful in his impersonation of a negro minstrel,” minstrel shows at Tanglin Barracks in 1904, RI’s 1925 magazine praising a student “garbed as a nigger minstrel,” and ads for “blackface favourites” in the 1930s—basically: you don’t get to call this “foreign” when it’s been locally documented since colonial Singapore.

Then the argument dies the way it always does: officials gesture at harmony while protecting majority comfort. Sharan drags Minister K. Shanmugam for questioning whether Singapore has the “context” for brownface because “no slavery,” and she counters with Singapore’s erased labour history (convict labour, mui tsai, Peranakan “slave wives”). She later documents how Preeti/Subhas get memory-holed when they do migrant worker fundraising—mainstream outlets ignore them, but their “troublemakers” label gets archived forever. Every year there’s a new flare-up (interracial dating harassment, “let’s talk about race” thinkpieces, paywalled handwringing), but the structure doesn’t change: minorities explain, majority whataboutism, state chills the conversation. Why care? Because this is the Singapore race discourse machine in miniature—how “we’re harmonious” gets maintained not by solving racism, but by outlasting the people who keep receipts.
